Chicago Food Inspections: Assessment 1 EDA¶

Predict whether an inspection will Fail, using information available before that inspection begins. The analysis uses a fixed local snapshot. Run from the project root or from base/ with the supplied data/ folder.

Analysis boundaries. Raw-data provenance, missingness and coverage are audited over the saved snapshot. Outcome comparisons and historical-feature exploration use inspections before 2025-01-01. The evaluation plan below records limitations from prior exploration of later outcomes. No model is trained here, and official hidden-period outcomes are never requested or used.

1. Load and verify the saved snapshot¶

A row is one inspection, not one establishment. Inspection ID identifies the visit; License # is an imperfect establishment identity key. Read licence numbers and ZIP codes as strings. A requested end date in a filename is not evidence that the snapshot contains records on that date.

The repository stores the raw CSV losslessly as .csv.gz. It is read directly, without manual extraction or downloads. A local uncompressed copy of the same snapshot is also supported. The SHA-256 check below always verifies the decompressed CSV bytes against the original downloaded file.

from pathlib import Path
import ast
import gzip
import hashlib
import json
import platform

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from IPython.display import display

SNAPSHOT_FILE = 'food_inspections_2016-01-01_2026-10-25.csv'
EXPECTED_SHA256 = '6ebba026f5b8f6c21c2b87efac548b14d0dff764175b706482b46e71e0b436ca'
TRAIN_END = pd.Timestamp('2024-12-31')
VALID_START = pd.Timestamp('2025-01-01')
TEST_START = pd.Timestamp('2026-01-01')
INTERNAL_END = pd.Timestamp('2026-09-30')
LABEL_MAP = {'Fail': 1, 'Pass': 0, 'Pass w/ Conditions': 0}

candidates = [Path.cwd(), Path.cwd().parent]
PROJECT_ROOT = next((p for p in candidates if any(
    (p / 'data' / name).is_file() for name in [SNAPSHOT_FILE, SNAPSHOT_FILE + '.gz']
)), None)
assert PROJECT_ROOT is not None, 'Run from the project root or base/ with the saved data/ folder.'
DATA_PATH = PROJECT_ROOT / 'data' / SNAPSHOT_FILE
if not DATA_PATH.is_file():
    DATA_PATH = DATA_PATH.with_suffix('.csv.gz')
META_PATH = PROJECT_ROOT / 'data' / 'download_metadata.json'
snapshot_open = gzip.open if DATA_PATH.suffix == '.gz' else open
with snapshot_open(DATA_PATH, 'rb') as stream:
    snapshot_hash = hashlib.file_digest(stream, 'sha256').hexdigest()
assert snapshot_hash == EXPECTED_SHA256, 'Snapshot changed: review the version before updating this notebook.'

raw = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH, dtype={'License #': 'string', 'Zip': 'string'}, low_memory=False)
meta = json.loads(META_PATH.read_text(encoding='utf-8'))
assert meta['csv_file'] == SNAPSHOT_FILE
assert meta['row_count'] == len(raw)
assert raw.shape[1] == 17

df = raw.copy()
df['Inspection Date'] = pd.to_datetime(raw['Inspection Date'], format='%m/%d/%Y', errors='coerce')
invalid_date_count = int(df['Inspection Date'].isna().sum())
assert invalid_date_count == 0, 'Investigate invalid dates before time-based analysis.'
assert df['Inspection Date'].between('2016-01-01', '2026-10-30').all()
assert df['Inspection Date'].between(meta['requested_window']['start_date'], meta['requested_window']['end_date']).all()
exact_duplicates = int(raw.duplicated().sum())
duplicate_ids = int(raw['Inspection ID'].duplicated().sum())
assert raw['Inspection ID'].notna().all() and duplicate_ids == 0
assert exact_duplicates == 0

df['fail'] = df['Results'].map(LABEL_MAP).astype('Int64')
labelled = df.loc[df['fail'].notna()].copy()
assert df['fail'].notna().equals(df['Results'].isin(LABEL_MAP))
assert labelled['fail'].eq(labelled['Results'].eq('Fail').astype(int)).all()

provenance = pd.DataFrame([
    ['Source', meta['portal_page']],
    ['Downloaded (UTC)', meta['downloaded_at_utc']],
    ['Requested window', str(meta['requested_window'])],
    ['Actual first inspection', str(df['Inspection Date'].min().date())],
    ['Actual last inspection', str(df['Inspection Date'].max().date())],
    ['Raw rows / columns', f'{raw.shape[0]:,} / {raw.shape[1]}'],
    ['Labelled / unlabelled rows', f'{len(labelled):,} / {df.fail.isna().sum():,}'],
    ['SHA-256', snapshot_hash],
], columns=['item', 'value'])
with pd.option_context('display.max_colwidth', None):
    display(provenance)
print('Python:', platform.python_version(), '| pandas:', pd.__version__, '| numpy:', np.__version__)
display(raw.head(3))

2. Missing values are not the same as invalid identifiers¶

isna() detects empty/NA values, not the literal number or string 0. A missing percentage rounded to 0.00% can still represent several records. Report both counts and sufficiently precise rates. The source does not tell us why zero licences were entered, so the decision below is a conservative identity policy, not a claim about the portal's official coding convention.

Official source check: the portal-linked data dictionary defines licence numbers as unique licensing identifiers but assigns no explicit meaning to zero. A saved copy is in data/documentation/food_inspections_data_dictionary.pdf; the online verification record is saved separately. Source checks occurred during preparation, not during this offline notebook run.

Policy: retain all visits and eligible labels. Use only positive, integer-form licence strings for linkage. Missing, zero or malformed licences have unknown identity, unavailable history and a separate flag. Do not group all zero/missing values together; do not infer aliases from names or addresses without validating a record-linkage method.

In [2]:
missing = pd.DataFrame({
    'missing_count': raw.isna().sum(),
    'missing_percent': 100 * raw.isna().mean(),
    'dtype': raw.dtypes.astype(str),
}).sort_values('missing_count', ascending=False)
display(missing.style.format({'missing_percent': '{:.4f}'}))

licence = raw['License #'].str.strip()
licence_number = pd.to_numeric(licence, errors='coerce')
missing_licence = licence.isna() | licence.eq('').fillna(False)
zero_licence = licence_number.eq(0).fillna(False) & ~missing_licence
valid_licence = (licence.str.fullmatch(r'[0-9]+').fillna(False) & licence_number.gt(0).fillna(False))
other_invalid = ~(missing_licence | zero_licence | valid_licence)
licence_status = pd.Series('valid_positive', index=df.index, dtype='string')
licence_status.loc[missing_licence] = 'missing'
licence_status.loc[zero_licence] = 'zero'
licence_status.loc[other_invalid] = 'other_invalid'
df['licence_status'] = licence_status
df['identity_unknown'] = ~valid_licence
df['establishment_key'] = licence.where(valid_licence)

licence_audit = df.groupby('licence_status', observed=True).agg(
    records=('Inspection ID', 'size'),
    distinct_names=('DBA Name', 'nunique'),
    distinct_addresses=('Address', 'nunique'),
).reindex(['valid_positive', 'missing', 'zero', 'other_invalid'], fill_value=0)
licence_audit['percent_of_all_records'] = 100 * licence_audit['records'] / len(df)
display(licence_audit.round(4))
print('Raw licence NA percentage rounded to two decimals:', round(100 * raw['License #'].isna().mean(), 2))
display(df.loc[zero_licence, ['Inspection ID', 'DBA Name', 'License #', 'Address', 'Results']].head(6))
assert df.loc[df.identity_unknown, 'establishment_key'].isna().all()
assert not df.loc[~df.identity_unknown, 'establishment_key'].eq('0').any()
assert licence_audit['records'].sum() == len(df)

Categories and geography: verify before simplifying¶

Apply fixed whitespace/case rules to facility and inspection types, without merging different business meanings. Preserve raw fields. Frequency-based category selection will use the training period only. City has both spelling variants and genuinely different city names: not every value is a Chicago typo.

Address is street/house-number text; ZIP is a postal area, not a community boundary. Location is a coordinate pair in this CSV. We check that it agrees with latitude and longitude before calling it redundant. Agreement does not establish geocoding accuracy. No community boundary file is introduced here.

In [3]:
def normalise_category(series):
    return (series.astype('string').str.strip().str.replace(r'\s+', ' ', regex=True)
            .str.casefold().replace('', pd.NA).fillna('Unknown'))

df['facility'] = normalise_category(df['Facility Type'])
df['inspection_type'] = normalise_category(df['Inspection Type'])
df['risk'] = df['Risk'].astype('string').str.strip().replace('', pd.NA).fillna('Unknown')
df['zip_category'] = df['Zip'].str.strip().replace('', pd.NA).fillna('Unknown')
category_audit = pd.DataFrame({
    'raw_nonmissing_categories': [raw[c].nunique(dropna=True) for c in ['Facility Type', 'Inspection Type']],
    'normalised_nonmissing_categories': [
        df.loc[raw['Facility Type'].notna(), 'facility'].nunique(),
        df.loc[raw['Inspection Type'].notna(), 'inspection_type'].nunique(),
    ],
}, index=['Facility Type', 'Inspection Type'])
display(category_audit)
display(raw['City'].value_counts(dropna=False).head(12).to_frame('records'))

parsed_locations = {}
for text in raw['Location'].dropna().unique():
    pair = ast.literal_eval(text)
    assert isinstance(pair, (tuple, list)) and len(pair) == 2
    parsed_locations[text] = (float(pair[0]), float(pair[1]))
pairs = raw['Location'].map(parsed_locations)
complete_coords = raw[['Latitude', 'Longitude', 'Location']].notna().all(axis=1)
lat_match = np.isclose(pairs.str[0][complete_coords].astype(float), raw.loc[complete_coords, 'Latitude'], atol=1e-9, rtol=0)
lon_match = np.isclose(pairs.str[1][complete_coords].astype(float), raw.loc[complete_coords, 'Longitude'], atol=1e-9, rtol=0)
coordinate_mismatches = int((~(lat_match & lon_match)).sum())
matching_coordinate_gaps = (raw.Latitude.isna().equals(raw.Longitude.isna())
                            and raw.Latitude.isna().equals(raw.Location.isna()))
assert coordinate_mismatches == 0 and matching_coordinate_gaps
print(f'Complete coordinate rows: {complete_coords.sum():,}; mismatches: {coordinate_mismatches}')
with pd.option_context('display.max_colwidth', None, 'display.max_columns', None):
    display(raw[['Address', 'City', 'State', 'Zip', 'Latitude', 'Longitude', 'Location']].head(3))
    display(raw.loc[raw.Latitude.isna(), ['Address', 'Zip', 'Latitude', 'Longitude']].head(3))

train_records = df.loc[df['Inspection Date'] <= TRAIN_END].copy()
eda = train_records.loc[train_records.fail.notna()].copy()
eda['fail'] = eda['fail'].astype(int)
training_fail_rate = eda.fail.mean()
print(f'Training-period EDA: {len(eda):,} labelled visits; Fail rate {training_fail_rate:.2%}')

3. EDA: eight figures tied to modelling questions¶

Dashed reference lines in the group-rate charts mark the overall labelled training-period failure rate; each group's denominator is its labelled visits.

Figure 1. Which outcomes become labels?¶

Comparison: training-period counts of all recorded outcomes. Colours distinguish Fail, non-Fail and excluded outcomes. Finding: non-Fail is more frequent than Fail; operational outcomes are not negative labels. Implication: accuracy alone can hide missed failures; use the specified Macro-F1 and retain earlier unlabelled visits as separate historical evidence. Limit: inspection counts are not counts of unique establishments.

Figure 2. Is time coverage stable?¶

Comparison: all raw monthly visit counts, plus annual failure rates only in the training period. Months without records are explicitly filled with zero. Finding: counts and training-period rates vary over time; the final month is only partly observed in this snapshot. Implication: preserve chronology, and do not compare a partial year/month to complete periods as if exposure were equal. Limit: counts alone cannot prove a reporting-lag duration or the cause of a drop. Future-period labels are not plotted here.

The official portal flags a 2018-07-01 inspection-procedure change. Treat this as a possible comparability issue across years, not proof that it caused any particular movement in failure rates.

Figure 3. Does missing violation text depend on the recorded outcome?¶

Comparison: the fraction with missing current-inspection Violations, within each training-period outcome. Finding: missingness differs substantially across outcomes. Implication: exclude the current text, its missing flag and any derived counts from predictors. Limit: association does not establish why text is absent. The exclusion is justified by the field's post-start timing, not merely by correlation. Historical violations would require separate timing and availability controls and are outside the proposed first baseline.

Figure 4. Does inspection type distinguish observed failures?¶

Comparison: within-type failure rates among labelled training visits, using normalised categories with at least 200 visits. Finding: complaint, licence, routine and re-inspection groups have different observed rates. Implication: inspection type is a plausible pre-visit categorical feature. Limit: this is not a causal effect or proof that it is the strongest predictor; selection processes and history also differ. Display cutoffs are not automatic modelling category-merging rules.

Reading the bars and dashed line. Each bar is the number of Fail visits divided by the number of labelled visits within that inspection type. The grey vertical dashed line is the overall 2016-2024 labelled-training Fail rate: 32,189 / 140,762 = 22.87%. It includes all training inspection types, including those not plotted. Bars to its right have higher observed rates; bars to its left have lower observed rates. This is a pooled, visit-weighted reference, not the unweighted mean of the plotted bars, a prediction threshold or a statistical-significance boundary. It does not adjust for other factors. The n >= 200 cutoff is a display choice to reduce small-group volatility and crowding, not a course rule or a guarantee of precision. Excluded categories and their records remain in the dataset.

In [7]:
def rate_table(frame, column):
    table = frame.groupby(column, observed=True)['fail'].agg(n='size', fail_count='sum', fail_rate='mean')
    assert (table.fail_count <= table.n).all()
    return table

def draw_rate_bars(ax, table, title, colour=BLUE, sort_by_rate=True):
    if sort_by_rate:
        table = table.sort_values('fail_rate')
    ax.barh(table.index.astype(str), 100 * table.fail_rate, color=colour)
    for y, row in enumerate(table.itertuples()):
        ax.text(100 * row.fail_rate + .5, y, f'{100 * row.fail_rate:.1f}% (n={row.n:,})', va='center', fontsize=8)
    ax.axvline(100 * training_fail_rate, color=GREY, linestyle='--', linewidth=1)
    ax.set(xlim=(0, max(100 * table.fail_rate.max() + 20, 45)), xlabel='Fail among labelled visits (%)', title=title)

type_stats = rate_table(eda, 'inspection_type')
shown_types = type_stats.loc[type_stats.n >= 200]
display(shown_types.sort_values('fail_rate', ascending=False).round(4))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 5.1))
draw_rate_bars(ax, shown_types, 'Figure 4. Inspection type (training n >= 200)')
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Figure 5. Risk grade and common facility types¶

Comparison: named risk grades and the ten most frequent normalised facility types in the training period. The latter are selected by frequency, not by high failure rates. Finding: recorded risk grades are not a simple ordering of observed failure probability; facility groups vary. Implication: retain them as candidate categoricals; learn rare-level rules on training data. Limit: these comparisons do not establish the official mechanism behind risk grades or explain the differences. The official data dictionary ties Risk to adverse public-health risk and inspection frequency, not a calibrated Fail probability. Missing categories are retained even when not among the categories plotted.

Reading the bars and dashed lines. A bar is the Fail proportion among labelled training visits in its risk or facility category; n counts visits, not unique businesses. Both grey dashed lines mark the same overall training reference, 32,189 / 140,762 = 22.87%. The reference includes every labelled training visit, including unknown Risk and facility types outside the ten displayed. It is not recomputed separately for each panel and is not an unweighted mean of its bars. A bar beyond the line is above the pooled rate; a bar before it is below. This visual comparison establishes neither a statistically significant difference nor a causal effect, and the line is not a model decision threshold. Facility categories are selected by visit count, then ordered by observed failure rate for readability.

Figure 6. ZIP-level variation, with both ends of the distribution¶

Comparison: highest and lowest eight failure rates among ZIP groups with at least 300 labelled training visits. The full eligible ZIP table is also shown. Finding: sufficiently represented ZIP groups differ. Implication: ZIP is a candidate area category, not an ordinal number. Limit: these are postal areas, not community boundaries; facility mix, inspection reasons and repeated establishments may explain part of the difference. This is not a causal ranking of neighbourhood hygiene. Coordinate value beyond ZIP remains untested.

Reading the bars and dashed lines. Each ZIP rate divides its Fail visits by its labelled training visits. Both panels use the same 0-60% horizontal scale and the same grey dashed reference: 32,189 / 140,762 = 22.87% across all labelled training visits. The reference includes visits with unknown ZIP and those in groups below the 300-visit display cutoff; it is not the mean of the selected high or low ZIP bars. Bars to the right of the reference are above the pooled rate and bars to the left are below. The line is neither a significance boundary nor a prediction threshold. Selecting extreme ZIP rates is descriptive, not an unbiased ranking of underlying area risk. The n >= 300 cutoff limits very small groups for display, does not guarantee precision and does not remove records from the dataset.

Figure 7. Strictly earlier-day history, without identity collisions¶

Aggregate visits by valid licence and date first. Cumulative counts exclude the entire current day, so changing the order of same-day inspection IDs cannot reveal another current-day result. History counts all past visits; failure-rate denominators count only past labelled visits. Unknown identities remain in the labelled dataset but are excluded from these history-group comparisons.

This is an EDA construction within the training period, not permission to update hidden-test history using hidden outcomes. With no dates before 2016 in our saved inputs, “no prior observed visit” does not mean “never inspected before”.

Reading the bars and dashed lines. Each bar measures the current Fail proportion among labelled, valid-identity training visits in that history group. The bars do not show historical failure rates. Both panels retain the same overall training reference as Figures 4-6: 32,189 / 140,762 = 22.87%, including the 325 unknown-identity labelled visits omitted from these bars. The reference is deliberately not recalculated on the history subset. Positions relative to it describe above/below-overall observed rates, not significance, causation or a model threshold. Counts and intervals follow their natural order rather than being sorted by failure rate.

In [10]:
def add_prior_day_history(records):
    valid = records.loc[records.establishment_key.notna()].copy()
    valid['labelled_visit'] = valid.fail.notna().astype(int)
    valid['failed_visit'] = valid.fail.eq(1).fillna(False).astype(int)
    daily = valid.groupby(['establishment_key', 'Inspection Date'], as_index=False).agg(
        day_visits=('Inspection ID', 'size'), day_labelled=('labelled_visit', 'sum'),
        day_fails=('failed_visit', 'sum'),
    ).sort_values(['establishment_key', 'Inspection Date'])
    groups = daily.groupby('establishment_key', sort=False)
    for source, target in [('day_visits', 'prior_visits'), ('day_labelled', 'prior_labelled'), ('day_fails', 'prior_fails')]:
        daily[target] = groups[source].cumsum() - daily[source]
    daily['previous_visit_date'] = groups['Inspection Date'].shift()
    daily['days_since_previous'] = (daily['Inspection Date'] - daily['previous_visit_date']).dt.days
    daily['prior_fail_rate'] = daily['prior_fails'] / daily['prior_labelled'].replace(0, np.nan)
    history_columns = ['prior_visits', 'prior_labelled', 'prior_fails', 'previous_visit_date', 'days_since_previous', 'prior_fail_rate']
    return records.merge(daily[['establishment_key', 'Inspection Date'] + history_columns],
                         on=['establishment_key', 'Inspection Date'], how='left', validate='many_to_one')

# Same-day results, unlabelled visits and invalid identities exercise different rules.
example = pd.DataFrame({
    'Inspection ID': [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6],
    'establishment_key': ['A', 'A', 'A', 'A', pd.NA, pd.NA],
    'Inspection Date': pd.to_datetime(['2024-01-01', '2024-01-01', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03', '2024-01-02', '2024-01-03']),
    'fail': pd.array([1, 0, pd.NA, 0, 1, 0], dtype='Int64'),
})
checked = add_prior_day_history(example).set_index('Inspection ID')
assert checked.loc[[1, 2], 'prior_visits'].eq(0).all()
assert checked.loc[3, 'prior_fails'] == 1 and checked.loc[3, 'prior_labelled'] == 2
assert checked.loc[4, 'prior_visits'] == 3 and checked.loc[4, 'prior_fail_rate'] == .5
assert checked.loc[[5, 6], 'prior_visits'].isna().all()
shuffled = add_prior_day_history(example.iloc[::-1]).set_index('Inspection ID').sort_index()
pd.testing.assert_frame_equal(checked.sort_index(), shuffled)

Figure 8. Does the Risk pattern persist within inspection types?¶

The earlier drafts noticed higher aggregate failure rates in the Low group. Instead of assuming a cause, compare the same four inspection types within each named risk grade. Show both rates and sample sizes; suppress cells with n < 100. Also standardise the rates to a common inspection-type mix in this restricted subset. This checks one compositional explanation, not all confounding.

Finding: the Low-versus-High difference is present within several inspection types; a common type mix changes the aggregate comparison but does not by itself explain away the pattern in the supported subset. Implication: retain Risk as a candidate category and investigate type/facility interactions rather than imposing a monotonic probability interpretation. Limits: this is descriptive standardisation over four types, not a causal adjustment or a model performance test. Facility mix, timing and inspection selection remain possible explanations.

4. Evidence-based data-quality summary¶

Counts below are computed from the saved snapshot unless explicitly marked training-period. “Possible reason” is a hypothesis. Repeated visits are valid observations; an identity or timing problem changes linkage, not automatically the eligibility of a supervised label.

5. Feature availability and evaluation population¶

A field can be allowed before inspection yet unnecessary for the first model. Excluding a field from model input does not mean deleting it from raw data. Identity-unknown visits remain eligible for prediction using other fields.

6. Modelling and evaluation plan (approximately one page)¶

Task and baselines. Predict Fail = 1 versus Pass / Pass w/ Conditions = 0. Compare an always-non-Fail reference with Logistic Regression. Start with normalised Facility Type, Risk, Inspection Type, categorical ZIP and calendar month/year. Compare adding prior-day counts, prior labelled failure rate, recency and explicit identity/history-availability flags. Unknown identities retain other predictors. Raw names, IDs, address text, current Results and current Violations (including missingness and derived values) are excluded. Coordinates are an optional later comparison; Location is redundant.

Preparation and history. Fit encoders, imputers, rare-level rules and any scaling on training only, with safe unseen-category handling. Treat Risk as categorical. Distinguish a valid key with no observed history, a valid key with no prior labelled visits, and unknown identity. Historical failure rates divide by prior labelled counts; do not fill undefined rates with an assertion of zero failure. Compare explicit missingness with smoothing toward a training-only base rate; fit smoothing strength inside chronological development folds. For a training row, any smoothing base rate must also come from an earlier development window. Only strictly earlier-day records may contribute history.

Time and information boundaries. Use 2016-2024 for training, 2025 for validation and 2026-01 through 2026-09 for internal model evaluation. Fix these windows before model experiments. Earlier drafts explored later-period outcomes, so the internal period is not claimed to be a wholly untouched test; disclose that limitation. Do not further tune based on its results. Inside training, use expanding time windows, with same-date records kept on the same side of each boundary. Compare model settings/class weights there; select the operating threshold on validation, beginning with 0.5. Freeze all choices before internal evaluation. For each scored validation/evaluation block, freeze outcome history at the block start rather than using earlier true labels from that scored block. This is conservative and matches batch prediction when block outcomes are not available. The official hidden window is separate; its outcomes are never used.

Groups, metrics and limits. Report Macro-F1 using the specified two-label calculation, plus per-class precision/recall/F1 and a confusion matrix. Also report known-history, unseen-valid-licence and unknown-identity groups when sample sizes permit. Licence overlap over time is not itself leakage; it tells us which deployment population is being evaluated. A missed Fail is an unflagged failed inspection; a false alarm flags an eventual non-Fail. Macro-F1 weights class F1 values equally, not operational costs. Associations concern inspected, labelled visits, not all businesses or causal effects. Nonstationarity, partial publication coverage, the 2018 procedure change, imperfect identity and absent pre-2016 history limit interpretation. No trained model or claimed performance is part of this A1 EDA.

7. Conclusions and submission checks¶

  • Correct labels and denominators matter: unlabelled operational visits are neither Fail nor non-Fail examples, but may describe eligible past history.
  • A displayed 0.00% missing rate and a literal zero licence are different issues. Counts reveal the first; identity auditing reveals the second.
  • Time, inspection type, facilities and postal areas show useful descriptive variation. Risk differences persist within several supported inspection types; the common-mix check narrows one explanation without claiming a cause.
  • Historical comparisons must exclude same-day outcomes and invalid-key linkage. Their candidate features need later time-respecting model validation.
  • Current-inspection Results/Violations and their post-start derivatives cannot be prediction inputs. Preserve the saved snapshot and audit trail.

Before submission: team members should review the revised choices and be able to explain the work; fill in the actual team names/IDs as required by the course platform; confirm the notebook and saved inputs are submitted/linked in the required repository structure. A later pre-cutoff refresh is optional, not a prerequisite; it requires explicit version changes and a full rerun. This notebook is an executed A1 draft, not a claim of guaranteed marks.
